meta.cite: Barton O. Oliver's mTOR Atlas (live data, not an archived version; give corpus_snapshot and source_commit). doi:10.5281/zenodo.22059963

data.mechanism: Genetic TORC1 inhibition in C. elegans extends lifespan through BOTH SKN-1/Nrf and DAF-16/FoxO, which activate protective genes and raise stress resistance. Rapamycin does NOT work the same way: it triggers a similar protective response but extends worm lifespan dependent on SKN-1 and NOT on DAF-16, apparently by interfering with TORC2 alongside TORC1 (ROB2012). This FoxO arrow therefore holds for the genetic arm, not for the drug.
data.mechanism_beginner: Part of how this pathway affects lifespan runs through stress-resistance genes switched on by FOXO – so far shown mainly in simple animals like worms, not yet in mammals.
data.boundary: An invertebrate result, and the two arms must not be merged. ROB2012's title reads 'TOR signaling and rapamycin influence longevity by regulating SKN-1/Nrf and DAF-16/FoxO', but its own abstract splits them: the DAF-16/FoxO requirement belongs to genetic TORC1 inhibition, while the rapamycin effect is SKN-1-dependent and DAF-16-INDEPENDENT. Not shown in mammals in this corpus.
